doc.title: Junior Mance Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 18, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]

title: How to teach the blues without getting technical
summary: He teaches the feeling rather than structure, and students keep returning; he limits class size by instrument.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Are you able to teach the blues and improvising without getting too technical with it? I’m not sure I asked that right.

You are saying it right. Because as I mentioned before, the last time, when they asked me to teach the blues, I said well how do you teach anybody to play the blues? And the answer was, oh you’ll find a way. Believe it or not I’m still looking for the right way, yeah. But actually I try to leave all the technical aspects out of it because then it becomes like a structured blues thing, which most of them already know. They know there is 12- bar blues, some of them don’t know that there are 8-bar blues and even 16-bar blues and 24-bar blues or 20-bar blues. But that takes no time to show them. So I stick with more the feeling, the spiritual or emotional side of it. And it works. And I guess I have sometimes the same students keep coming back. I’ve had students who come back all four years. And these are like the better students, the A students, and they keep coming back. And I find myself, I don’t know whether this sort of pushes me a little bit to come

up with different ideas. But I do each semester. And I think this is why it’s still fun to me. And I’ve asked different students, why do you keep coming back? Oh man, we love this class, we learn something every time. And it’s for all instruments, not just piano. You know it’s an ensemble. That’s why they changed the name of it to ensemble because we usually have enough people like for a band. I had to sort of put a clamp, a cap on it, because sometimes I was stuck with like six piano players. The class is two hours long and everybody’s not going to get a chance to play. So now I limited it to two piano players, two drummers and two bass players so they can trade off. Horns I sort of am a little looser on that, because that’s always different. Like last semester I had four saxophone players and four trumpets which was great. But the thing we’re short of, strangely enough in the school, is trombone players. There are only two trombone players in the whole school.
